raw_response:
I'm a 47-year-old farmer in Quzhou County with primary school education and 30 years of farming under my belt. I farm 10.1 mu of land with wheat-maize double cropping. My household has 8 people, and some of my family work off-farm jobs, which brings in extra cash but also means I can't always count on family labor when I need it most.

**What I'm thinking about for this year:**

It's early October now, so it's time to plant winter wheat. I've been doing this wheat-maize rotation for decades. Last year my wheat yielded about 400 jin per mu (roughly 400 kg/mu), which was okay — not great, not terrible. The maize did a bit better, maybe around 450 kg/mu. This year I'm hoping for similar or slightly better if the weather cooperates.

For the wheat, I'll plant around mid-October, maybe the 12th or 15th, depending on when the soil is ready. My neighbor down the road, Old Wang, he's planting a few days earlier this year because he says the weather's been warm, but I think I'll stick to my usual timing. I've got an improved wheat seed variety that I've been using for a couple years now. It costs me about 25-30 yuan per mu for seed. I don't save my own seed anymore — bought seed just grows better.

For fertilizer, I usually put down one bag of compound fertilizer per mu as base fertilizer before planting — that's about 50 kg per mu of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer, which gives me some nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Then at jointing stage in spring, I'll topdress with about 20-25 kg of urea per mu. So in total, that's probably around 15-16 kg of actual nitrogen per mu, plus whatever's in the compound fertilizer for P and K. I know the extension people say I could use less, but honestly, I'm scared to reduce too much. Last year I tried cutting back a little on one plot and the wheat looked yellow. I'd rather waste a bit of money on fertilizer than risk losing yield. My family needs the food security.

I'll irrigate the wheat three times: once in winter if it's too dry (around New Year), once at jointing, and once at heading. Water costs money — electricity for the pump isn't cheap — but you can't skip it if there's no rain. Each irrigation costs me roughly 15-20 yuan per mu.

For pesticides, I'll spray herbicide once after planting to control weeds, and maybe an insecticide if I see aphids in spring. I don't spray fungicide unless there's a real problem.

For maize, the challenge is always the tight turnaround after wheat harvest in early June. There's no time for proper tillage — I either no-till plant right behind the combine or do one quick pass with the rotavator. I'll plant hybrid maize seed, costs a bit more, about 35 yuan per mu, but it pays off. For fertilizer, I put compound fertilizer in the planting hole or beside the seed, then topdress with urea at the big trumpet stage (when the leaves are big). That's about 14 kg N per mu total. I'll irrigate twice if it's dry — once at the V6 stage and once during flowering.

Labor is tight because my sons work in the factory in town. For wheat harvest and maize planting in June, that week is brutal. I'll probably hire 2-3 days of labor to help with harvest and planting, plus maybe 2 days for maize harvest in fall. Family labor handles the rest — my wife and I, plus whoever is around. Family labor is maybe 15 days for wheat total across the season, and 12 days for maize. Hired labor costs about 100-150 yuan per day.

Money is always the constraint. With 10.1 mu, I've got to watch every yuan. I can't afford to be the best-equipped farm, but I've got my own small tractor and access to the village's tube well for irrigation. Total input costs for both crops will probably run me about 5,500-6,000 yuan for the year. That's a lot of money for me, but if I can get 420 kg/mu on wheat and 480 kg/mu on maize, I should come out ahead after selling the grain.
